@@130949935 <h> The UN 's unhappy birthday <p> The United Nations , which has just turned 80 , has seldom looked as precarious as it does today <p> How was the UN created ? Initial planning began in 1939 , when it became clear that the League of Nations had failed in its job of preventing another world war . The term " united nations " was first used by Franklin D. Roosevelt , in a 1942 declaration by 26 nations that pledged to fight against the Axis powers . The UN 's basic shape was hammered out by " the Big Four " -- the US , the USSR , Britain and China -- at a conference in Washington DC in late 1944 -- and agreed by Roosevelt , Churchill and Stalin at the Yalta Conference a few months later . In April 1945 , representatives of 50 nations ( and 80% of the world 's population ) met at the United Nations Conference on International Organisation in San Francisco to draft and ratify the charter . Pledging to " save succeeding generations from the scourge of war " , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ does it look like today ? Headquartered in New York , the UN now has 193 members and an annual general budget of $3.72 billion . Its peacekeeping forces have 60,000 military personnel stationed around the world . The UN asserts that it is " neither a supra-state nor a government of governments " . Rather , it sees itself as a forum for international dialogue and cooperation . Its charter sets out four main purposes , from maintaining peace and security to promoting social and cultural cooperation . It retains the basic structure agreed at Yalta . The General Assembly is " the world 's parliament " , where each nation can discuss important issues and vote on equal terms . But the real power lies with the Security Council , which is designed to take " prompt and effective action " in response to any emergency ; it can order sanctions , blockades and military action to uphold decisions . It is comprised of the " Big Five " permanent members ( the " Big Four " plus France ) , each of which has the power of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ ) . What has the UN achieved ? It has codified a body of international laws and forged the 1948 Universal Declaration of Human Rights . It played an important part in decolonisation -- Article 1 of the charter recognised the right of self-determination -- and is credited with brokering more than 170 peace settlements ; its peacekeeping forces have helped end conflicts from Colombia to Sierra Leone , Burundi to Cambodia . The World Health Organization ( WHO ) , a UN agency , played a leading role in the eradication of smallpox in 1980 , a disease that had killed 300 million people in the 20th century alone . It has helped broker international deals , such as the 1970 Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons Treaty and the Paris Climate Accords . No nation has used a nuclear bomb since 1945 ; to its supporters , the UN is still the best defence against world war . <p> Have there been failures , too ? Certainly . The UN 's nadir arguably came in 1994 , when peacekeepers in Rwanda failed to prevent the genocide of some 800,000 Tutsis @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ 8,000 Bosnian Muslims were massacred in Srebrenica by Bosnian Serbs while Dutch peacekeeping troops stood by helplessly . The UN has also been plagued by allegations of sexual abuse by peacekeepers , known as " Blue Berets " . More fundamentally , though , the UN 's own structures -- primarily the Security Council veto -- often prevent action . <p> How does the veto cause problems ? The veto ensured the participation of the major powers in the UN ( the US had never joined the League of Nations ) . But the flip side is that the Security Council has been paralysed by vetoes . In total , more than 320 resolutions have been vetoed -- most often by Russia ( or the USSR ) and the US , though China is now a frequent blocker . The USSR , for instance , vetoed objections to its 1979 invasion of Afghanistan ; the US has vetoed nearly 50 resolutions on Israel alone . British , French and US vetoes stopped the UN condemning apartheid in South Africa . Indeed , arguably the Security Council has worked only as @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ invaded by the North in 1950 -- and then only because the USSR was boycotting the UN , and China had yet to take the Security Council seat from the Republic of China ( Taiwan ) . The second was after the invasion of Kuwait by Iraq in 1990 , at a brief high point in East-West relations . But though the UN has always wrestled with such structural flaws , it is now facing difficulties of potentially even greater magnitude . <p> Why is it in difficulties now ? It seems increasingly a spectator in a might-is-right world . Russia 's invasion of Ukraine in 2022 made a mockery of the principle of respect for national borders . Israel 's war against Hamas in Gaza proceeded despite resolutions from the General Assembly demanding a ceasefire and thunderous condemnations from the UN Secretary-General Ant ? nio Guterres . The UN has seemed unable even to intervene in wars in which great powers are not involved , such as Sudan 's civil war . Developing countries regard it as being biased in favour of the West , while Brazil , Russia @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ as a potential rival . And perhaps most damagingly , US conservatives regard the UN as both irrelevant and too partial to progressive causes . <p> Why is that so damaging ? Because the UN has always relied so heavily on American power and money ( it funds over 20% of the UN 's regular budget ) . The Trump administration is now planning a more than 80% reduction in UN funding next year . The US is already withdrawing from the Paris climate deal , the WHO and Unesco , among other organisations . Republican lawmakers have introduced more than 20 pieces of legislation targeting the UN , and US participation in it . Though it retains considerable global legitimacy , and its programmes still perform crucial roles around the world , the UN is -- financially and operationally -- in deep crisis.The architecture of the UNThe UN has five principal " organs " ( originally six , but one , the Trusteeship Council for managing former colonial possessions , is now " inactive " ) . The General Assembly is made up of representatives from all 193 member @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ budget , elect non-permanent members of the Security Council , and appoint the secretary-general . The Security Council has " primary responsibility for the maintenance of international peace and security " . The UN Secretariat is the office of the secretary-general , its highest official , who is appointed for a five-year , renewable term . The International Court of Justice is the only one of the bodies not located in New York ( it sits in The Hague ) ; it is responsible for adjudicating legal disputes between countries . Finally , the Economic and Social Council is responsible for coordinating the economic , social and related work of 15 UN specialised agencies , from Unesco to the International Monetary Fund to the Food and Agriculture Organisation . In addition , there are a series of autonomous " subsidiary organs " , funds and programmes , such as the World Food Programme and the United Nations Development Programme . Daily attacks under the surface that the public is only vaguely aware of . <p> Keir Starmer has acknowledged that the UK faces a threat " more serious , more immediate and more unpredictable than at any time since the Cold War " , and vowed to prepare this country for the fight . <p> Labour 's Defence Select Committee chair Tan Dhesi warns that " we are not in a state of readiness " and declares that " our government needs to do more " -- both in terms of putting us on a war-footing and raising awareness about the level of threat we are under . <p> " The Prime Minister needs to lead that national conversation , " Dhesi tells The House . " <p> A recent wave of crippling cyber-attacks on major UK businesses , most notably Jaguar Land Rover ( JLR ) but also the Co-op and Marks &amp; Spencer , has brought attention to this vulnerability . <p> " We saw with JLR , for example , and many other businesses have been impacted . The MoD itself has had , I believe , about 90,000 different attacks in the last couple of years . " <p> The National Cyber Security Centre is reportedly investigating Russia as the possible culprit behind the JLR attack . <p> " It 's too early for people like myself just to come out with our own conclusions , " Dhesi replies @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ responsible . People loved it . They looked forward to it like the Morecambe and Wise Christmas special -- or at least the Christmas edition of the Radio Times . It became an end-of-year staple . <p> Around the world , I had journalists I spoke to once a year @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . I had a regular slot on BBC News . I gained thousands of social media followers . <p> So why give all that up ? <p> There are a number of reasons this year 's montage will be the last . I never wanted it to become a chore . I used to put them together in a week or so , but now it takes more and more time each year . <p> The number of people included has more than doubled since the first one . I do n't think twice the number of people have died ; I 've just become more completist about it . <p> It has fans who feel ownership over it . If I miss their personal favourite , they get upset . I do n't like upsetting people , so I work much harder now -- and that 's a lot of pressure . <p> Ten seems like a good , round number . I said in 2016 I 'd never do it again -- and again in 2018 , 2019 . I do n't want to do it forever . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Personally , it would be a bit much if I ended up doing a Sgt Pepper montage with Damon Albarn and Jarvis Cocker on the front row . <p> As a friend once said , what are you going to do -- keep going until one year you leave it half-finished and someone has to add you into it ? I 'm sure AI will be able to make them soon anyway , and people can just pop a spreadsheet into ChatGPT and create their own montage -- avoiding any debate about who goes where . <p> The main reason I 'm stopping this year is Charlie Kirk -- or , more specifically , my shock at the reaction to his death . Society has changed a lot in the last ten years . <h> Suggested Reading <p> Looking back at the montages from 2016 -- 2024 is like a visual history of how the world has evolved . They cover everything from Covid to Gaza , the Queen dying to Grenfell Tower . Researching them for my upcoming book reminded me of stories I might otherwise have forgotten . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ shifted . I included a poppy on the Sgt Pepper drum in 2018 to commemorate 100 years since the end of WWI . I probably would n't do that now . Society has become so polarised that even the poppy -- a neutral motif of remembrance -- has been distorted into a symbol of militarism and nationalism . <p> So , why Charlie Kirk ? I 'll be honest : I was n't very aware of him before he died . I 'd seen the memes , but I did n't realise how influential he was . When he was shot , I thought , ' well , I wo n't include him ' . Every inclusion , every position is an editorial choice after all . I decide who goes where depending on my view , and if I do n't want to include this minor far-right agitator , that 's up to me . <p> But the way the Trump administration , the right-wing press , and -- frankly -- the mainstream media covered his death took me by surprise . We 're so far down the rabbit @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Charlie Kirk , that would become the story and overshadow everything else . That 's too much pressure . This was supposed to be a bit of fun . <p> Chris Barker 's 2024 montage <p> It feels like you have to be on one team or the other now . The fact that I worried about what the right wingers might make of my decision to exclude Kirk -- and what left wingers would say if I included him -- was an indicator that maybe it was time to call it a day . @@131085786 <h> As a homesick Palestinian-Jordanian , these are my favourite Arabic restaurants in central London <p> When I first moved to London from America , my teta ( grandmother ) said she no longer needed to pack spices and herbs into my suitcase before travelling , because ingredients for the best Arabic food could be found on one street : Edgware Road . @@131088442 <p> The British Labour Party has reportedly abandoned its 2019 definition of Islamophobia , opting instead for a new formulation centred on " anti-Muslim hate " . <p> According to a report in the Telegraph , the revised wording , yet to be officially released by the government , omits all references to " Islamophobia " . <p> The earlier definition , developed by the All-Party Parliamentary Group on British Muslims and widely endorsed by the Muslim Council of Britain , numerous civil society organisations and experts , characterised Islamophobia as " a type of racism that targets expressions of Muslimness or perceived Muslimness " . <p> The new draft , replacing the term " Islamophobia " with the alternative " anti-Muslim hatred " , makes a distinction that is not merely linguistic , but politically and globally consequential . <p> Terminology determines whether discrimination is approached as an issue of individual prejudice , or as a manifestation of systemic , racialised power embedded in national and international structures . <h> New MEE newsletter : Jerusalem Dispatch <h> Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Islamophobia has grown out of decades of advocacy , scholarship and lived experience among Muslim communities . It names a reality that victims themselves recognise ; a reality that connects their everyday encounters of suspicion , exclusion and violence to wider systems of power . <p> The proposed shift would erase that recognition , denying Muslims the political language through which they have made their experiences visible and credible . In comparable cases , such as antisemitism and anti-Black racism , the importance of naming has long been accepted . <p> I approached the Labour Party for a comment but received no answer until time of publication . <h> Structural phenomenon <p> These other terms are not routinely questioned , replaced or redefined by government committees . Indeed , shortly before his election as British prime minister , Keir Starmer had no qualms using the term " Hinduphobia " in addressing the concerns of the British Hindu community . <p> To strip the term Islamophobia of legitimacy would be to treat Muslim suffering as somehow exceptional - as something still up for debate , rather than something the world already @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ hatred " individualises what is in fact a structural and collective phenomenon . It frames hostility towards Muslims by limiting it to moral or psychological terms , as an expression of intolerance or bias that can be remedied through education or hate-crime interventions . <p> Using the term Islamophobia exposes how discrimination is embedded not at the margins of the state , but within its core practices of governance <p> This depoliticised framing isolates anti-Muslim racism from its institutional and ideological roots , confining responses to the realm of interpersonal civility and policing , rather than addressing systemic injustice . By locating the problem in individual emotion rather than in the political and structural constitution of Muslim marginalisation , the revised term ultimately obscures the operation of power . <p> Islamophobia captures how Muslims are racialised ; imagined as a distinct and inferior civilisational category . This framing allows for the recognition of Islamophobia as a form of racialised governance , in which Muslims are managed , surveilled and disciplined through political , media and bureaucratic institutions . <p> Scholarship over the years has repeatedly demonstrated that Islamophobia functions analogously @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ exclusion , producing Muslims as a suspect category incompatible with alleged British values . <p> The distinction between the two terms also has significant political implications . The notion of anti-Muslim hatred restricts attention to hate crimes and community cohesion programmes , while Islamophobia demands engagement with institutional complicity and structural racism . <p> The latter directs analysis towards state policies , such as Prevent and other counterterrorism strategies that normalise suspicion of Muslim populations . Using the term Islamophobia exposes how discrimination is embedded not at the margins of the state , but within its core practices of governance . <h> International resonance <p> Islamophobia operates as a global formation of power that produces Muslims as racialised subjects across diverse geographies , from immigration regimes in Europe to security policies in Asia and North America . This shared language of suspicion and control has been tragically exemplified in the ongoing genocide in Gaza , where the dehumanisation of Palestinians relies on Islamophobic tropes , casting Muslim mobilisations as fanaticism and Muslim lives as disposable . <p> The Gaza genocide thus reveals the global reach of Islamophobia ; it is @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ that legitimises the mass suffering of Muslim populations under the banner of security , civilisation or self-defence . <p> Finally , the term Islamophobia has achieved broad international recognition , having been adopted by the United Nations , the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation , and major human rights and civil society groups around the globe . <p> In contrast , the term " anti-Muslim hatred " lacks such international resonance or conceptual rigour . Its institutional adoption would thus represent not a neutral linguistic adjustment , but a symbolic and political regression with regards to both the global consensus , and the intellectual and activist labour that has made visible the systemic nature of Islamophobia . <p> In sum , Islamophobia is a more rigorous and globally recognised concept that encapsulates the structural , ideological and transnational dynamics of anti-Muslim racism , while " anti-Muslim hatred " reduces these dynamics to questions of personal sentiment . <p> The choice of terminology is therefore not merely linguistic , but profoundly political , as it defines whether Muslim suffering is understood as incidental prejudice or a feature of the modern global system @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ is about whose reality counts . To call out Islamophobia is to see the full picture , from the classroom to the newsroom , from the UK borders to Gaza . Replacing this term after decades of activism and recognition would not be neutral ; it would be erasure at the highest levels . <p> The views expressed in this article belong to the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial policy of Middle East Eye . <p> Shaheen Kattiparambil is a lecturer in the School of Sociology and Social Policy at the University of Leeds <p> Middle East Eye delivers independent and unrivalled coverage and analysis of the Middle East , North Africa and beyond . @@131193149 <h> Interview : Cardinal Vincent Nichols as he turns 80 years old <p> Cardinal Vincent Nichols has led the Catholic Church in England and Wales for more than fifteen years , guiding it through a period of rapid social change , deepening secularisation but also renewed evangelisation . <p> Born in Crosby on 8 November 1945 and ordained to the priesthood in 1969 , he has served as Archbishop of Westminster since 2009 , and was created a cardinal by Pope Francis in 2014 . " We 're going to start an education centre , " she said . " And you 're going to come and see the Director of Education . " <p> So the Director of Education was duly rung up -- his name escapes me now . And she said , " This @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ see you with Father Nicholas . In the intervening years , he joined other political campaigns and worked as a foreclosure-prevention counsellor , working to help families keep their homes . <p> Yet the help he could offer was few and far between - constantly constrained by a system designed to disadvantage the working class . <p> He concluded that dispossession occurred " because the state has allowed big capital and financial speculators to run amok within the housing market " . <p> Helping people required a reconfiguration of the laws . He ran for office . <p> " After decades of slashing taxes to line the pockets of the rich , New York State faces a politically manufactured budget deficit . To solve it , we need elected officials who have the political courage to raise taxes on the wealthy and corporations to fund the life-saving public goods and services @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the actor , and progressive New York City politician , said , as she became among his earliest endorsers . <p> Upon becoming an assembly member in late 2020 , Mamdani looked to shift the debate on transit fares , on power plant justice - he fought against creation of a natural gas plant in Queens - and debt relief for taxi drivers . <p> It spoke of a man invested in economic justice , working through the mechanisms of the law - though he at times gestured toward more radical means to house those in need . <p> As an assembly member , his stint was n't particularly spectacular . But much of his work focused on coalition-building and shaping discourse , rather than signing bills that did little to advance a working-class agenda . <p> In the weeks following my first call with him , New York City , like the rest of the world was gripped by the Covid-19 pandemic . The pandemic ripped through the working class in the city . <p> Neighbourhoods like Queens and the Bronx were particularly impacted as working class families struggled @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ that made social distancing impossible , or through the shut down of sections of the regular economy . <p> Mamdani found himself in the middle of it . <p> " The life has been taken out of the neighbourhood , " Mamdani told me in April 2020 as the city heaved under the pandemic . <p> " I was speaking with a Bangladeshi taxi driver just about last week , and he told me that he has n't been able to work for already three weeks . <p> " It makes you realise that this pandemic is blind to the realities of our society , but those realities dictate how people are impacted , and how long it will take them to be able to recover from this , whether it is medically , financially , mentally - all of these sorts of things - and I think that these pre-existing fault lines in our society have dictated that certain communities are being disproportionately hit by this disease , " Mamdani added . <p> Meanwhile , the work continued at Albany . <p> Among the few bills he did help @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ a public hearing ; minor , but subtly more democratic . <p> Later , he introduced the symbolic " Not on Our Dime ! : Ending New York Funding of Israeli Settler Violence Act " , which sought to block $60m in funding to Israeli settlements in the West Bank . <p> The bill was shut down by local politicians almost immediately - but the response revealed the power of spectacle . The story drew headlines . <p> It was his intervention , however , the fight to secure debt relief for taxi drivers in 2021 , through the auspices of a 15-day hunger strike outside City Hall , that put him on the map . <p> " I will lay down my life for him , " Momoudou , a New York City taxi driver who had been initially been lumped with $750,000 debt , said of Mamdani following its successful alleviation . <p> Still , Mamdani remained a largely local figure outside his neighbourhood of Astoria and the Democratic Socialists of America ( DSA ) in New York . He was , however , quietly building a name @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ boldly on affordability and , crucially , Palestine . <p> And then came the events of 7 October 2023 . <h> The genocide in Gaza <p> The devastation of Gaza - to lives , homes , places of worship , refugee camps , hospitals - and the complicity and support for Israel by the then US president Joe Biden 's administration - catalysed what would become known as the biggest anti-war movement since the 1960s over US involvement in Vietnam . <p> As early as 13 October 2023 , Mamdani began expressing fears over the danger of a genocide in Gaza . <p> " We are witnessing a genocide and humanitarian crisis in Gaza . Hospitals have run out of painkillers , and bodies are being stored in ice cream trucks . We are calling for a ceasefire because it is the only way to stop the killing and provide humanitarian aid , " Mamdani would add on 20 October 2023 . <p> During this period , New York City became a focal point of pressure campaigns demanding that universities , cultural institutions and media organisations answer for their complicity @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ crisis fractured the self-professed moral authority of the western cultural establishment ; institutions such as The New York Times appeared not as guardians of public conscience , but as active participants in the repression of dissent . <p> While Republicans and the mainstream Democratic leadership doubled down in support of Israel 's right to defend itself , progressive figures such as Bernie Sanders and Alexandria Occasio-Cortez ( AOC ) largely hesitated , unable or unwilling to offer moral clarity to a generation appalled by the assault on Gaza . <p> These came as a death knell to progressive Democratic politics in the US . <p> The genocide had rendered them peripheral , even irrelevant figures . <p> When AOC took the stage at the DNC in August 2024 and described Kamala Harris as " working tirelessly to secure a ceasefire in Gaza and bring the hostages home " , it signalled her final shift from insurgent outsider to party loyalist . <p> Describing it as a betrayal , Kareem Elrefai , a New-York based organiser with the DSA wrote that Gaza " was a red-line , defining issue of our @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ side of it " . <p> Mamdani emerged out of this wreckage . <p> His early and consistent naming of the assault as genocide , his criticism of the crackdown on student encampments , and his solidarity with those vilified in the press won him admirers . <p> His position in a hyper-local , multi-racial , immigrant , working-class district - where tenants , taxi drivers and small shop owners lived the consequences of US foreign and domestic policy - gave him political cover to take such stances . <p> Whereas national leaders wavered , Mamdani , along with several activists , including the actor Cynthia Nixon , launched a hunger strike outside the White House , where in icy conditions , they urged Biden to alter course on Gaza . <p> " We hunger-strike not because we want to . We hunger-strike because we have been forced by this president and by our government 's foreign policy . We hunger-strike because Palestinians have been doubted in life and death , and their experience has been erased , " Mamdani said at the time . <p> But the spectacle raised @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the US government . He was part of a national story . <p> Back in New York City , the protests for Palestine had long reached a crescendo . <p> Students who had protested for Palestine had been suspended ; academics fired or their reputation dragged through the halls of Congress ; even restaurant workers who dared to show support for a people being annihilated faced persecution . And underneath it all , activists continued to link the affordability crisis with the prioritisation of the US military industrial complex . <p> If public resources can fund foreign military projects , why ca n't they fund housing and social services here ? <p> Mamdani found himself at the intersection of that question . <h> The run for mayor <p> In the summer of 2024 , Mamdani began exploring a run for mayor . <p> Fahd Ahmed , executive director of Drum Beats , a group widely credited for being instrumental in Mamdani 's successful run for mayor , told me that when Mamdani approached the organisation last year to talk about a potential run for office tailored to the material interests @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ They had seen how he had worked with the Taxi Workers Alliance ; they knew he was willing to take risks , but also willing to work collaboratively . <p> After a vetting process , Drum Beats was among five organisations , including Worker Families Party ( WFP ) and the Democratic Socialists of America ( DSA ) , that endorsed him from day one . <p> Ahmed described taking the campaign into communities as " exhilarating . " <p> " It deeply resonated , because it speaks to the material issues of working-class communities , and because it 's willing to speak to other larger issues of our communities that historically nobody 's willing to touch , like Palestine , like right-wing Hindu forces , " Ahmed said . <p> Ahmed said it was n't easy getting support from some community leaders . Many felt it was impossible . But grassroots enthusiasm outpaced caution , forcing leaders to choose between joining or being left behind . <p> ' Mamdani is interesting , and I think more thoughtful than his detractors would suggest ' <p> - David Axelrod , former @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ crisis - the inability to pay rent , buy groceries , accumulate savings - was driving people of colour towards the right because they were at least talking about the ills of the system . <p> But the right wing - as embodied by figures such Donald Trump - were weaponising people 's disgruntlement with corporate takeovers , and militarism , by pushing people to turn on each other . Mamdani 's focus on the economy was a winner . <p> " It does n't mean that we are sidelining the other issues , but we want to lead with the material issues - rent , groceries , housing , transit , " Ahmed said . <p> In October , the announcement came that Mamdani was running for mayor of New York City with three promises : freezing the rent for rent stabilised tenants ; free childcare ; making buses fast and free . <p> At the time , Mamdani was polling at 1 percent . His candidacy felt like a test run . But he had other plans . <p> Mamdani 's team unleashed a thunderous social media campaign @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ captured the imagination of a discerning New York public itself . <p> A neglected electorate facing ICE raids , a cost-of-living crisis and high rents , yearned in search of deliverance ; Mamdani rose to the occasion . <p> It was n't just what he was promising , but how he made those commitments . <p> He was fresh , energetic . He was earnest . His promises were straightforward and uncomplicated . <p> It was genius . Mamdani 's team managed to adapt his politics to the media of the day - TikTok , Instagram , X , WhatsApp - engineering his message to the logic of the platform . He prioritised influencers , cultural-specific content that spoke uniquely to different communities , in several languages too . <p> His message leaned on cultural representation , drawing on the levers of Bollywood , warm inviting typography , and humour ; while never letting go of the pedal : making NYC affordable . <p> Offline , he committed to knocking on a million doors . Observers say the canvassing was extraordinary . <p> He made politics - out of reach @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . He spoke with them about the issues that concerned them ; and they felt heard and seen . <p> It should n't have even been a contest with Cuomo , the independent candidate backed by Trump , given the history of corruption , the death of the elderly during Covid 19 under his watch , the sexual allegations pitted against him . <p> But given the sheer idiocy of American politics , Cuomo came with wealth , name recognition and billionaire backers - he had to be defeated . <p> Still , the more Mamdani emerged as a viable challenge , the trickier it would become . <p> By then , Mamdani had already secured the youth and a large majority of the left in NYC . <p> Given the large-scale disappointment on the left with AOC and Sanders , their endorsement felt less like authentic popular leadership and more like catch up . <p> Others saw it as an attempt to rehabilitate their own reputation , and critically , the reputation of the Democratic Party that had been dragged through the mud over its pro-corporate , anti-working class @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ <p> Following his victory in the Democratic Primary that made him the Democratic Party candidate for mayor , Mamdani reportedly received a call from former US President Barack Obama . <p> Obama is said to have , according to the New York Times , " offered him advice about governing and discussed the importance of giving people hope in a dark time , according to people with knowledge of the conversation " . <p> As if on cue , Mamdani began consolidating his team with former Obama aides floating into his orbit . <p> Jeffrey Lerner , the former Democratic National Convention ( DNC ) director , joined as his communications chair . <p> The appointment raised some eyebrows , especially given Lerner 's colourful work history , including working for Cuomo in 2007 . <p> Then there were reports that Zara Rahim was hired as a consultant to work on digital strategy . Rahim previously worked as a digital director for Obama . Later she served as a spokesperson for Hillary Clinton . <p> Soon enough , sections of the establishment appeared to constrain and discipline his language ; @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ looked to appear reasonable , palatable , to some of the very issues that had given a boost to his campaign . <p> Through looking to work with establishment Democrats , and creating a transitional team of City Hall veterans and non profit executives , he promised continuity . <p> Mamdani met with business leaders to assuage their fears and Obama aides , including Patrick Gaspard - the national director for former President Obama 's 2008 presidential campaign - introduced him to other city power brokers . <p> " I went over and he , indeed , is interesting , and I think more thoughtful than his detractors would suggest , " David Axelrod , CNN chief political analyst and former senior adviser to President Obama said of his meeting with Mamdani , as arranged by Gaspard . <p> " I told Mamdani that I do n't agree with every proposal he has , but I know he is asking the right questions , " Axelrod added . <h> Shifting rhetoric <p> By September 2025 , Mamdani was no longer the insurgent assembly member from Astoria with socialists , Arab @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ primary focus . <p> He was running for mayor of one of the most intensely pro-Israel political environments on the planet . <p> Things , it appears , would have to be adjusted , to win . <p> First , he apologised for comments he made previously about the police being racist and calls to defund the police -from 2020 , in which he also said , " There is no negotiating with an institution this wicked and corrupt . " <p> But he went beyond simply softening his stance on the police . <p> He said would let the current police commissioner , Jessica Tisch - an avowed pro-Israel supporter who has also led mass surveillance against NYC 's Muslim communities - an issue that helped promulgate his run for office in the first place - stay on next year . <p> Then , after being questioned repeatedly about Israel 's ' right to exist ' , he conceded that it had the right to exist as a state where all people were equal . <p> Organisers wished he had adopted the obvious position : no state had the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ like Israel . <p> ' His backtracking on his pro-Palestinian stance disappointed me ' <p> - Cassandra , 21-year-old New Yorker <p> Some of his supporters argued that by calling for equal rights , he was calling for the dismantlement of settler-colonialism . <p> This perspective however , ignores that the call for equal rights does n't address the fundamental nature of dismantling settler-colonial rule : the question of land back . <p> Mamdani was also harassed over the slogan " Globalize the Intifada " ; he promised to discourage it . <p> He cited a rabbi 's fear that the phrase would provoke attacks in New York - here centering Jewish communal anxieties at a moment when Palestinians were being killed in overwhelming numbers . <p> Then , he said he would hire people in his administration with whom he disagreed with on Israel , focusing on competence over alignment . <p> He also gently walked back on his vow to arrest Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu as mayor of New York City , arguing that he would act within the bounds of the law . <p> Though his @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ is not a signatory to the ICC - that he would feel the need to correct the record appeared designed to placate . <p> The language shifted in other ways , too . <p> During the Hindu festival of Diwali , he visited a temple and said that while he opposed Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi 's Hindu nationalist policies , he understood that there were people in New York " who may feel differently than me about Mr Modi , and that 's their right , and I will look to represent them all the same , because my responsibility to them as New Yorkers is to ensure that they are safe , to ensure they can afford this city " . <p> Mamdani earns endorsement from influential Orthodox-Jewish community leader in NYC <p> The usually incisive Mamdani appeared to be stretching his coalition outward in ways that risked diluting the internationalist commitments that once grounded his politics . <p> If his project was to defend those targeted by structures of racial and economic domination , then one had to ask : where are the boundaries of that protection @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ rhetorical tent ? If not , why then would Hindu nationalists or Zionists be welcome ? <p> As someone who started an SJP chapter at his college , attended scores of rallies for Palestine , who also supported anti-Hindutva protests in New York City - some began to question how he could then pander to the very Zionists and Hindu nationalists responsible for reinforcing domestic support for ethnonationalist regimes abroad . <p> And it 's been a question on my mind for months . <p> Earlier this year , when Mamdani attended an interfaith Eid gathering at the Indian consulate in NYC , I asked him to clarify why he would go to an Eid event hosted by the Indian government . <p> " Celebrating the spirit of Eid with unity , gratitude , and joy ! " the consulate boasted on its social media platforms . <p> I asked him if he would attend an Eid event at the Israeli embassy in New York City , knowing how the Israelis were treating Muslims and Palestinians . <p> He did n't reply . <p> Mamdani 's purported attempt to separate @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ to build a broad base of support is not just a denial of the forces of history that elevated him to this moment , but a misreading of how local bread and butter issues were inextricably linked to US imperial matters . <p> But Ahmed from Drum Beats says that criticism needs to be weighed proportionally . <p> " Are there any other major electoral races that have emerged where somebody has taken a sharper line and demonstrated success with it ? The answer is no , " Ahmed added . <p> The veteran organiser says the Islamophobic attacks and accusations of antisemitism that Mamdani faced over the past would have been even more intense had he refused to make some concessions . Mamdani had also faced a barrage of attacks from the Hindu right wing , too , for having spoken about Modi , or for previous attendance at anti-Hindutva rallies . <p> As the argument goes , Mamdani , did n't disavow Palestine or say he would stop talking about Hindu nationalism . He only tweaked his approach . <h> New York 's first Muslim mayor <p> On @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ of New York City . <p> His election was watched across the US , in South Asia and the Middle East , in Uganda and South Africa . <p> The optics of a South Asian , Muslim and immigrant to have captured NYC a mere two decades after the events of September 11 that had given rise to the so-called War on Terror that killed close to a million people worldwide - many of whom were Muslim - carried its own symbolism . <p> Was his victory a crack in the US empire ? Or was this a classic case of America 's enduring capacity to neutralise dissent through inclusion - where those who begin by challenging the system eventually help sustain it ? <p> A hint of what might come emerged from Mamdani 's victory speech , where he quoted a section of the address given by the first Indian prime minister , Jawaharlal Nehru , at the dawn of the creation of India in 1947 : " A moment comes but rarely in history , when we step out from the old to the new , when an @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ suppressed finds utterance . Tonight , we have stepped out from the old into the new , " Mamdani narrated . <p> But did Nehru take India from the old to the new ? <p> For those who know - including most likely Mamdani himself - Nehru was an upper-caste Brahman , who oversaw a structure that did n't truly bring real decolonisation and continued many of the functions of the colonial apparatus - but , this time , with a brown man in charge . <p> He occupied Kashmir , forcibly annexed Hyderabad and disrupted movements for self-determination in the North East , and subordinated popular movements across the country in the name of modernity . <p> By drawing on Nehru , Mamdani appeared to disavow any prospect of real change in NYC . He appeared to be offering a facade of change . <p> And indeed , Mamdani 's victory is not the first history-making event in US politics . Rashida Tlaib , AOC , Ilhan Omar , and before them , Obama , were heralded as transformative . <p> They , too , were deified by fans @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ in different degrees , have had to dance to the tune of US foreign policy or the Democratic establishment . <p> And it 's not as if the signs are going by unnoticed . <p> " His backtracking on his pro-Palestinian stance disappointed me . I recognise the political pressure in New York , where even minimal solidarity with Palestinians draws severe backlash and violent threats , but I wish he had stayed firm , " Cassandra , a 21-year-old student from New York City who asked to be identified by her first name , told me . <p> " The genocide against Palestinians has only worsened , and it is crucial that Palestinian communities in New York feel seen , supported , and safe , " she said , adding that she voted for Mamdani based on his consistent position on improving the standard of living in the city . <p> Cassandra said her family were recipients of food aid and during the federal shutdowns , the delays had consequences for the wellbeing of the household . <p> Mamdani 's promises had the potential to transform their lives . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Alina , who asked to be identified only by her first name as well , told me that she , too , was unhappy with his backtracking . <p> " I do n't know if it 's because of the egregious amounts of Islamophobic campaigns that were launched against him , but I wish he would 've just stuck with his original stance . Sticking with it would have shown an even stronger message . " <p> " But he 'll also get accountability from us , " she added . <p> But therein lies another conundrum . It is unclear how Mamdani might be held accountable , or to whom . <p> For all the accusations that he is a communist or a radical , Mamdani is a democratic socialist - where there is an emphasis on government taking more control on critical economic levers like transport , or energy , or health , that benefits the public instead of corporations . <p> The idea is to build a more inclusive economic order , not necessarily transform it . <p> Although he had the support of organisations such as @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , he ultimately ran on his own platform , not as a representative of a disciplined membership formation . <p> There is , as of yet , no organisational structure capable of setting collective priorities or binding him to a shared programme . <p> In practical terms , there is no educational or political spine to the movement that elevated him : no cadre development , no mass assembly , no mechanism of recall . <p> What exists instead is a constellation of door-knocking networks , viral social media currents , and a sense of shared-identity . <p> For many , he is the young man who speaks about Palestine , brings warmth , and looks like the people he claims to represent . <p> But without a democratic organisation to which he is meaningfully accountable - one that can set policy collectively and insist that its representatives remain tethered to the movement 's horizon - Mamdani , or more precisely the people who voted for him , face a profound challenge . <p> The coalitions that helped bring him to power are now left to the mercy of his @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ admit this is something they are still trying to resolve . <p> So have New Yorkers been duped by a polished , sophisticated outreach campaign ? <p> Not exactly , says Nazia Kazi , an associate professor of anthropology at Stockton University , who has written extensively about Muslims in the US since the events of 11 September 2001 . <p> She told me the problem was rather that " Americans are not taught to ask savvy questions . " <p> Kazi points to Mamdani 's hiring of Lerner , the former Democratic National Convention ( DNC ) director , as his communications chair as an example of a development that has n't been probed enough by his supporters . <p> " Just over a year ago , the DNC was the site of delegates covering their ears as protesters read the names of children killed by Democrat-provided bombs in Gaza . <p> " What does it mean for Mamdani to say he 'd like to continue working with Jessica Tisch the New York Police commissioner who presided over the crackdown at Columbia University and has been an outspoken supporter @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ does it mean that people who raise these timely and pragmatic questions are dismissed outright , accused of trying to impede a movement rather than propel it ? " Kazi asked rhetorically . <p> It is unclear how Mamdani would respond if mass mobilisation were directed against his administration - particularly given his stated commitment to staffing his government based on technical competence rather than ideological alignment . <p> " It 's not just that the ruling class allows glimmers of critique or dissent ; it 's that these glimmers then serve a very real function , which is to tame and redirect people 's political energies into the orbit of the two party system , " Kazi added . <p> Ahmed , from Drum Beats , however is still hopeful , but conceded that the moment did demand a careful balance between external pressure and internal governance . <p> City organisers who came out to canvas , and voters , too , remain hopeful that Mamdani will stay committed to the project that carried him into office - but in a vacuum of organisational accountability , the pull of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ has reshaped politicians more experienced than him . <p> " If Mamdani can get free buses and affordable childcare into New York - great . @@131204068 <h> World War I : Worcestershire Yeomanry role at Charge at Huj <p> This article is brought to you by our exclusive subscriber partnership with our sister title USA Today , and has been written by our American colleagues . It does not necessarily reflect the view of The Herald . <p> AT this time of the year our thoughts turn to Remembrance . <p> We remember those who were killed or whose lives were changed as a result of conflict . <p> If we think back to the Great War in particular , our minds are often filled with the images of trenches , mud and the stalemate on the Western Front . <p> We may also think of the Worcestershire Regiment and battles such as Gheluvelt . <p> However , our very own mounted regiment , the Queens Own Worcestershire Hussars or the Worcestershire Yeomanry as they are often called , fought a very different war in the desert and mountains of the Middle East , a theatre often seen as a sideshow of the main war . <p> The wide-open spaces made it ideal for using mounted @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ which gave them the ability to cover a large amount of ground quickly . <p> They could charge on horseback with their swords in hand but could also dismount and fight on foot with their rifles and bayonets if required . <p> The yeomanry was first sent to protect the important Suez Canal as part of the Egyptian Expeditionary Force ( EEF ) . <p> They spent a short and unhappy time away from their horses while fighting in Gallipoli but were soon repatriated with their brave war horses for the push east through the Sinai Desert and into Palestine . <p> On October 31 , 1917 , the EEF broke through the Ottoman defensive lines running across southern Palestine from Gaza to Beersheba . <p> The race was on to reach Jerusalem and Jaffa . It was important to keep the enemy on the run to prevent them from forming a new , and possibly stronger , defensive line . <p> The yeomanry was part of the 5th Mounted Brigade which also included the Warwickshire Yeomanry and Royal Gloucestershire Hussars . <p> They were unleashed to keep the enemy @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ However , as the main Ottoman Force continued to retreat east , around 2,000 Turkish and Austrian infantry began to make a stand across three low ridges near Huj . <p> This rearguard also included heavy machine guns and various pieces of artillery . <p> In the early hours of November 8 the 5th Mounted Brigade were watering their horses in the Wadi Barada . <p> As the sun rose squadrons from the Warwickshire Yeomanry and Worcestershire Yeomanry began moving ahead of the 60th ( London ) Division . <p> By midday , while resting behind a low ridge , they could hear the sound of enemy artillery firing on the infantry to their rear . <p> A dusty staff car then appeared , bouncing towards them from the column under attack . <p> It was carrying General John Shea , officer commanding the 60th Division . <p> He explained his men were being shelled and it would take them at least an hour to close on the enemy position , taking heavy casualties every step of the way . <p> He requested the yeomanry should launch an attack immediately @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Yeomanry , was in command and began to plan the attack . <p> In total 190 officers and men on their horses formed up and began to move toward three key objectives using all available cover . <p> The overall attack at Huj was described by Lt Mercer : " Machine guns and rifles opened up on us the moment we topped the rise behind which we had formed up . A whole heap of men and horses went down 20 or 30 yards from the muzzles of the guns . " <p> Lady Butler , the famous war artist , painted the victorious charge showing the yeomanry overrunning the enemy guns . <p> The details match the accounts which talk of the enemy fleeing or hiding from the swinging swords between their silenced guns and limbers . <p> Of the 190 men who took part in the charge , 36 lay dead and 57 were wounded . Three out of four squadron commanders were killed leading their men . <p> The Worcestershire Yeomanry suffered by far the worse casualties . <p> Out of 105 officers and men 19 were @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ 17 killed and 18 wounded out of 85 in total . <p> Over 100 horses were killed or had to be destroyed as a result of their horrific injuries . <p> Several enemy guns were captured . <p> Four Krupp 75mm field guns , four mountain guns and three 5.9-inch howitzers had been captured plus four heavy machine guns and about 80 Austrian and Ottoman soldiers . <p> Roughly 90 enemy soldiers had been killed , including from the cut and thrust of the yeomanry swords . <p> It took time to treat and evacuate the wounded and to bury the dead . <p> The yeomen who had been killed were buried in a mass grave . <p> A memorial was later made by the brigade 's farriers and erected over the grave in February 1918 . <p> After the war the bodies were exhumed and reinterred in Gaza War Cemetery . <p> Major Oscar Teichman , the medical officer for Worcestershire Yeomanry writing in the Cavalry Journal in 1936 , said : " The Charge at Huj , had it occurred in a minor war , would have gone @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ at Balaclava . <p> " In the Great War when gallant deeds were being enacted on all fronts almost daily it was merely an episode but , as the official historian remarks , ' for sheer bravery , the episode remains unmatched ' . " <p> At the time the charge at Huj was only referred to as ' The Affair at Huj . ' <p> To the yeomanry and their families , the charge was a bloody battle fought many miles away from their loved ones and beautiful Worcestershire . <p> It succeeded in pushing the Ottomans back and would help bring the war to an end . <p> As we pause to remember , I encourage everyone to remember the battle that is almost forgotten in Worcester . <p> The brave Charge at Huj , the yeomanry and their gallant war horses should be remembered with pride . <p> The affair at Huj also has the distinction of being the last unsupported cavalry charge made by the British Army . <p> To learn more about Worcestershire Yeomanry , visit The Commandery which will be the new home of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ This website and associated newspapers adhere to the Independent Press Standards Organisation 's Editors ' Code of Practice . It is highly controversial because of the risks it poses to women and children . <p> But the BBC 's coverage of gender ideology too often takes as fact the quasi-religious belief everyone has @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ that to dissent is bigoted . <p> This has led the BBC to ignore altogether important national stories about children 's healthcare , such as the young people who have detransitioned after irreversible hormone treatment . The EGSC is the senior forum in which we scrutinise BBC output when concerns have been raised ( from either internal or external sources ) and where we determine what action needs to be taken . Put simply : the Committee 's job is to examine the bad news not the good news . Sometimes the mistakes are one-offs , others may point to underlying problems . The job is never complete . But it is only by identifying and highlighting these issues and implementing changes that the BBC demonstrates its commitment to continuous improvement . <p> There is another view that has gained currency in the coverage that the BBC has done nothing to tackle these problems . Action in these areas ranged from published corrections and clarifications to new editorial guidance being issued . In other cases considered by EGSC , disciplinary action has been taken . <p> On top of the specific stories , EGSC also identified concerns about underlying problems -- for example in the Arabic service or long form journalism . These two areas have been discussed at length at the EGSC and action has been taken to tackle this kind of problem . @@131236841 <h> Two heads rolling wo n't stop rot at the BBC <h> The corporation 's mindset is hermetically sealed and can not cope with any dissenting view <p> The resignation of the BBC 's director-general Tim Davie and its most senior news executive Deborah Turness was as inevitable as it was startling . It was inevitable because of one revelation in particular in the explosive memo that found its way into the press last week . <p> The memo was written by Michael Prescott , a former member of the Beeb 's standards committee . It revealed that Panorama had doctored a quote by Donald Trump ahead of the fateful riots against the US Capitol on January 6 , 2021 . It had spliced together two different bits of his speech to give the false impression that he had directly encouraged the violence , when in fact he had urged his supporters to " peacefully and patriotically make your voices heard " . The White House has denounced this as " purposeful dishonesty " and threatened legal action . <p> The BBC chairman , Samir Shah , has now acknowledged @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ in a way which " did give the impression of a direct call for violent action " . That was rather more than an error of judgment . It was journalistic fraud and character assassination . <p> Prescott 's memo , however , was far broader and even more devastating . Drawing upon internal reports that he said were ignored , he revealed that on issue after issue the BBC 's reporting had been biased , untruthful or grossly misleading . <p> A unit of rogue LGBT+ reporters had been censoring coverage of the trans debate ; the BBC had sought out non-expert academics to produce a simplistic and distorted narrative about British slave-trading ; and even its own fact-checking service , Verify , produced a " thoroughly wrong " report suggesting car insurers were racist . <p> In its wider reporting , the BBC had implied Israel had committed a war crime when it suggested the IDF had buried hundreds of bodies in mass Gazan graves , even though the same BBC reporters had reported extensively on Palestinians who had dug those graves at the time . <p> Shah @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and speed up the complaints process , would reshuffle a string of executive chairs and had restructured BBC Arabic . None of this is adequate . It is vanishingly unlikely the BBC can ever understand what it 's done . <p> Since the furore exploded , BBC staff and their media and political allies have been circling the wagons with claims that it is all a political move by people who want to bring the corporation down . The fact that the memo revealed the BBC had demonstrably betrayed its own charter principles of impartiality , fairness and truth is dismissed . It 's being portrayed as giving into Trump , or to a cabal of rightwing forces , or to the Jews . Everyone else is to blame but never themselves . <p> That reaction itself illustrates the institutional leftism that 's the real problem here . The arrogance of the Panorama team that doctored Trump 's words reflected their confidence that this would never be challenged because the BBC hierarchy all shared the same premise . People who in this world-view are wicked beyond measure -- Trump , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ -- are axiomatically beyond the pale . Whatever they do or say is wholly without merit or justification . So painting them in the worst possible light can not be unfair , and claims about them that are untrue ca n't be lies . <p> Advertisement <p> BBC executives , like many if not most of its journalists , believe this left-wing mindset is the political centre ground and thus embodies balance , fairness and truth . Anyone who challenges that mindset is therefore axiomatically regarded as an extremist or hopeless partisan and is self-righteously ignored.This is a hermetically sealed thought system . It grips not only the BBC but the universities and great swathes of the administrative class , the professions and the rest of civic and public life -- including those whose names are now swirling as Davie 's possible replacement . <p> No 10 has said the prime minister does not believe the BBC is " institutionally biased " and that it was right to continue to support the BBC , particularly " in an age of disinformation " . Much of the public has already lost trust in it . A significant and growing number of people are quietly refusing to pay the licence fee . People are increasingly getting their news from podcasts , videos and social media . @@131261846 <p> As the BBC 's director general and head of news resign amid an uproar over a misleadingly edited speech by US President Donald Trump , the narrative seems neat : an error , consequences , accountability . <p> But this latest scandal was prompted by the wrong controversy . <p> While headlines continue to focus on a single editing mistake , the real crisis at the heart of Britain 's public broadcaster runs far deeper , most notably in its failure to report Israel 's war on Gaza with honesty or courage . <p> And the irony is brutal : the BBC has been shaken by one of the smallest of its sins , while the greater one - its distortion of Palestinian reality - goes unpunished . <p> The scale of that failure is measurable . A stunning report by the Centre for Media Monitoring , which analysed more than 35,000 BBC items published between October 2023 and May 2025 , showed that the corporation 's coverage of Gaza consistently privileged Israeli perspectives , while marginalising Palestinian voices . <h> New MEE newsletter : Jerusalem Dispatch <h> Sign @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters <p> The data is devastating . Palestinian deaths , reported as more than 42,000 during the study period , received 33 times less attention per incident than Israeli deaths . The BBC used words like " murder " 220 times for Israelis , but just once for Palestinians , and " massacre " 18 times more often for Israeli victims . Israeli officials and commentators were interviewed more than twice as often as Palestinian ones . <p> Even when reporting on humanitarian suffering , Palestinians were portrayed as passive victims - displaced , starving , dying - and rarely as people with rights , history or agency . Only 0.5 percent of reports referenced Israel 's decades-long occupation , and a mere two percent mentioned the word " apartheid " , despite its use by major human rights organisations . <h> Institutional bias <p> As the Centre for Media Monitoring concluded , the BBC has repeatedly adopted the language and framing of the Israeli state , while neglecting the voices of those under its occupation . That is n't impartial journalism ; @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ balance " . <p> Yet the rightwing gaslighting and attempts to distort reality have not ceased . Two years ago , I wrote about how Israel 's complaints against BBC coverage were " being cynically exploited in a domestic culture war " . Each accusation of bias becomes a weapon for Britain 's right-wing politicians and pundits , who want to cow the broadcaster into permanent caution . <p> The BBC has spent the last year doing just that : appeasing the loudest voices , rather than standing by its journalists or its duty to report the truth . <p> Honesty starts with saying : we got it wrong - not in a film edit , but in how we told , and continue to tell , the story of an entire people <p> The resignations of BBC News CEO Deborah Turness and director general Tim Davie underscore this contradiction . @@131409016 <h> Article 18 -- a forgotten human right ? <p> Following the horrors of the Second World War , the newly formed United Nations decided that humanity needed a common set of principles to govern individual rights . <p> A committee of representatives from around the world , led by Eleanor Roosevelt , the former First Lady of the United States , was established . This committee subsequently produced a document that became the Universal Declaration of Human Rights . <p> Its 30 articles cover everything from the right to property , a fair trial , and free assembly to -- importantly , for those of us who have faith -- Article 18 , which protects the right to freedom of religion or belief . <p> But what do we mean by religious freedom ? His Holiness Pope Leo spoke passionately on the importance of religious freedom in an audience with Aid to the Church in Need before the launch of our latest report into religious freedom . Pope Leo said , " Religious freedom , therefore , is not merely a legal right or a privilege granted to us @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ authentic reconciliation possible . When this freedom is denied , the human person is deprived of the capacity to respond freely to the call of truth . " <p> Quoting the late Pope Francis , Pope Leo said : " Indeed , as my venerable predecessor observed , ' there can be no peace without freedom of religion , freedom of thought , freedom of expression and respect for the views of others ' ( Francis , Urbi Et Orbi , 20 April 2025 ) . " <p> Pope Leo made it clear that " For this reason , the Catholic Church has always defended religious freedom for all people . " <p> He added : " The Second Vatican Council , in Dignitatis Humanae , declared that this right must be recognised in the legal and institutional life of every nation ( cf. 7 December 1965 , 4 ) . The defence of religious freedom , then , can not remain abstract ; it must be lived , protected and promoted in the daily lives of individuals and communities . " <p> But whilst the theory of religious freedom @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ And what is the state of religious freedom in the world today ? <p> Unfortunately , our latest Religious Freedom in the World Report published in October paints a bleak picture for the status of this fundamental human right . According to our research , nearly 2/3rds of humanity live in countries where there is a risk of religious persecution . <p> Of this huge mass of human souls , 413 million Christians live in countries where religious freedom is severely violated -- with , approximately 220 million living in countries where they are directly exposed to persecution . 62 countries around the world have some form of persecution or discrimination against minority faith communities . 24 of those are listed places where faith is actively persecuted . <p> But what are the key drivers of persecution and how is this allowed to happen when freedom of religion or belief is viewed as a fundamental human right ? <p> The right to worship , to practice your faith , in private or communally , is fundamental to the human dignity . @@131445592 <p> When Fahad Ansari set off for home from a family holiday in Ireland , the last thing he expected was to be surrounded by police officers and detained in front of his wife and four children . <p> For more than two decades , Ansari has defended those at the sharp end of the UK 's counterterrorism apparatus - clients stripped of British citizenship , detained without charge , or threatened with deportation based on secret evidence . <p> But this time , Ansari found himself targeted by the same laws he has spent decades describing as " unjust " and " corrupt " . <p> " They wanted to make an example of me , " Ansari told Middle East Eye in an exclusive interview . <p> " This was not about security . It was about intimidation -- a message that anyone who challenges state power can be treated as a suspect . " <h> New MEE newsletter : Jerusalem Dispatch <h> Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine , alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters <p> For Ansari , the detention @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ solicitor who has represented politically sensitive clients for decades , he believes the state targeted him not just as a citizen but in response to his legal work -- most notably deciding to represent the Palestinian militant group Hamas pro bono in its bid to challenge its proscription as a terrorist organisation in the UK . <p> " They were sending a message to lawyers like me : challenge the system and you will be scrutinised , " said Ansari . <p> ' They were sending a message to lawyers like me : challenge the system and you will be scrutinised ' <p> -- Fahad Ansari <p> Last August , Ansari had been driving home with his family after a short break in Ireland , where he grew up , when North Wales Police pulled them over at the port of Holyhead as they disembarked from the ferry . <p> Ansari initially thought it was a routine stop , but within minutes it became clear that something else was happening . <p> North Wales Police informed him that he was being detained under Schedule 7 of the Terrorism Act , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ <p> The measure allows police and border officials to stop , question and search individuals without suspicion -- often for hours -- and seize their personal devices in the name of finding terrorists . Refusing to comply is deemed a criminal offence and can result in imprisonment . <p> " My four children were watching from the back seat , " Ansari recalled . <p> " They saw their daddy being treated like a criminal . That 's the image they 'll remember -- not the holiday , but police surrounding our car . " <h> Sensitive legal information at risk <p> While the police claim that Schedule 7 does not target individuals , Ansari felt otherwise when he saw his car 's registration number written on the hand of one of the officers who detained him . <p> During his three-hour detention , the police took a DNA sample and his fingerprints , and confiscated his phone , telling him to deactivate the device 's face ID and pin code or face arrest . <p> Ansari was particularly concerned that sensitive , legally confidential information on his phone could @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ putting his clients at risk . <p> Officers went on to question him about his hobbies , what books he read , his views about Palestine Action -- the direct action group opposing the UK 's complicity in Israel 's genocide in Gaza , and which in July was controversially proscribed as a terrorist organisation -- as well as asking him about the mosques he attends , the war on Gaza , pro-Palestine protests he attended , and Hamas . <p> Ansari thought the worst was behind him . Then his daughter 's phone pinged days later , with a message saying her father was trying to access it . There was one problem : Ansari 's phone was still with the police . <p> " That 's when I knew the police were actively going through my phone , " said Ansari . <p> " It 's one thing to target me , but to try to target my daughter ... it made me angry more than anything else . " <p> For Ansari , the experience was chilling , but an eye-opener into what his clients go through @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ " Hearing about my client 's experiences is one thing , but having to be in their situation is completely different , " said Ansari . <p> " I was taking mental notes for my clients on how to help them when they encounter this situation . " <h> Legal challenge <p> The experience led Ansari to launch legal action challenging his Schedule 7 stop and the police 's right to access his phone , arguing that such access would breach legal privilege , which protects confidential communication between lawyers and their clients and is a cornerstone of the British justice system . <p> While the judicial review is set to take place early next year , Ansari 's legal challenge has already hit a stumbling block , after the High Court denied him interim relief . <p> ' When you do this kind of work ... your family feel it too -- every stop , every stare , every time the doorbell rings unexpectedly ' <p> -- Fahad Ansari <p> That ruling meant police-appointed solicitors could access Ansari 's work phone without his consent in order to assess what @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Once that line is crossed , it undermines the entire foundation of trust between a lawyer and their client , " said Ansari . <p> " How can anyone accused of terrorism or political offences expect a fair hearing if their solicitor knows their private communications could end up in the hands of the very agencies prosecuting them ? " <p> Ansari believes the episode was prompted by his role representing Hamas in its bid to be de-proscribed as a terror organisation . <p> He has made clear that he has taken no money from Hamas , given that taking funds from a proscribed organisation is illegal under British law . <p> But he acknowledges that working on the case , based on questions of international law and the UK 's complicity in Israel 's war on Gaza , has come at a heavy personal cost . <p> " After I agreed to take on the case , I could feel the pressure building , " he said . <p> " Friends warned me it would make me a target . My family was worried about what it might mean @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ it placed on his wife and children , who had to live with the anxiety of knowing their father 's work could draw unwanted attention from state authorities . <p> " When you do this kind of work , it does n't just affect you , " he said . " Your family feel it too -- every stop , every stare , every time the doorbell rings unexpectedly . " <h> ' Everyone deserves a lawyer ' <p> Since the start of the Hamas case , Ansari said he has received hundreds of death threats and been forced to adopt security measures to protect his family . <p> But he stands by the fundamental importance of his work . <p> " If people lose the right to be represented then what are lawyers for ? Are we just here for people who have n't committed crimes ? " said Ansari . <p> " Paedophiles , terrorists , murderers -- they all have lawyers . War criminals have lawyers . Since then , their football has offered little of major note - but in this instance , quiet is a good thing . <h> Yugoslavia <p> Yugoslavia was banned from the 1994 FIFA World Cup due to United Nations sanctions imposed amid the escalating Yugoslav Wars . In May 1992 , UN Security Council Resolution 757 prohibited the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia ( Serbia and Montenegro ) from participating in international sporting events as part of broader economic and diplomatic measures against the country for its role in the conflicts in Bosnia and Croatia . <p> This effectively barred their national football team , which had qualified for the tournament through earlier rounds , from competing in the finals held in the United States .

@@131473110 <h> Grand Egyptian Museum gala : An imperial spectacle haunted by history <p> In decades past , lavish parties have been used to prop up regional regimes - shortly before their downfall <p> Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi poses with officials and guests during the opening ceremony of the Grand Egyptian Museum in Giza on 1 November 2025 ( Egyptian Presidency/AFP ) <p> The historical significance and civilisational contributions of Pharaonic Egypt are beyond dispute . But the recent opening ceremony of the Grand Egyptian Museum was not a cultural celebration of ancient glory . It was a political affair and , contrary to appearances , a symptom of compromised sovereignty and national underachievement . <p> The lavish gala , held on 1 November against the backdrop of the Giza pyramids , bore all the hallmarks of political propaganda in modern history . Similar high-profile spectacles have been staged in the past to prop up regimes during times of subservience to foreign powers , growing dependency on private money or extractive wealth , and increasing unpopularity at home . <p> At the time of their execution , these vanity fairs @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ of surplus power and renewed legitimacy . In retrospect , they were telltale signs of these regimes ' decadence and eventual demise . <p> One of the most famous instances took place in Egypt itself more than 150 years ago . In 1871 , Cairo hosted the opera Aida to global acclaim . The opera was composed by Italian superstar Giuseppe Verdi and commissioned by Egypt 's then-ruler , Khedive Ismail , to celebrate the opening of the newly built Suez Canal . <p> A century later , the shah of Iran , Mohammad Reza Pahlavi , threw a regal party among the ancient ruins of Persepolis to commemorate the 2,500-year anniversary of the reign of Persia 's powerful king , Cyrus the Great . <h> New MEE newsletter : Jerusalem Dispatch <h> Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine , alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters <p> The inauguration of the Grand Egyptian Museum , not to be confused with the museum itself , was not a reproduction of either . None of these events were similar , but all three expressed dominant historical @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ consumption . <h> Colonial culture <p> European taste in fashion , food and music - and even the reimagining of history - was omnipresent in Aida and the shah 's Persepolis festival . As Edward Said explained in his analysis of Aida as an imperial spectacle , Verdi insisted on constructing a set whose " temples and palaces had to be reproduced in an orientation and perspective staging the actuality of ancient Egypt as reflected through the imperial eye " . <p> The khedive 's taste for European art and his entourage of European advisers did not save him from deposition by the West <p> The storyline was chosen by French Egyptologist Auguste Mariette , head of Egyptian antiquities under the khedive . The plot , Said tells us , was imbued with European stereotypes of the exotic and despotic Orient . <p> Some of the male priests were converted in the script into priestesses . For Said , this reflected the conventional European tradition of centring the " Oriental woman " in any exotic practice . On stage , these priestesses were functionally equivalent to dancing girls , slaves @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ bonanza was almost entirely a European affair . In order to erect a tent city in the wilderness to house and entertain dozens of foreign dignitaries , the shah flew in everything and everyone - from trees , to trays , to chefs , to waiters - from European capitals . <p> European taste was also visible at the Grand Egyptian Museum event . Classical European music dominated scenes of dancers dressed in ornate pharaonic costumes . The operatic genre soared in many languages . In line with American globalised culture , emphasis was placed on an international outlook that fused performances from Brazil to Japan into the programme . <p> Rather than calling for their repatriation , obelisks removed from Egypt during colonial times - and which are now standing in Paris or New York - were peddled as evidence of Egypt 's far-flung influence . <p> Largely absent were Egypt 's contemporary repertoire of Arabic music and rich tradition of Islamic art , both of which made only ephemeral and symbolic appearances . The emphasis on a pre-Islamic past and a Europeanised present is a fixture of colonial @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ <p> The exorbitant costs associated with these events are another sign of the age of decadence they embody . The opera house built by the khedive under the supervision of Italian engineers is estimated to have cost ? 16.5m ( $21.8m ) . Verdi , who confessed in a letter to his friend that he had " never been able to admire " Egyptian civilisation , agreed to write a special opera in return for the hefty sum of 150,000 francs in gold . <p> The khedive 's reckless spending on the opera was emblematic of his temperament . His tenure was known for its grand construction projects at a time of increasing concentration of wealth through the consolidation of land ownership , corvee labour , and other forms of burdensome taxation whose impact fell squarely on peasants and workers . <p> His splurging habits , often fuelled by corrupt European advisers , contributed to the ballooning of public debt . The latter led to the eventual bankruptcy of Egypt and its occupation by British forces . The khedive 's taste for European art and his entourage of European advisers @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ <h> Swept from power <p> The shah 's desert party at Persepolis was no less of a wild splurge .
